question: Why did customers who left decide to leave?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every stated reason the customer gives for leaving or planning to leave OrbitFlow, including the decision maker's explanation, any competitor they moved to or considered, specific product gaps, pricing or budget issues, support or onboarding problems, and any hedges or contributing factors. Also note any OrbitFlow staff response to these reasons.
assumptions: Scope limited to the Churn post-mortem calls (CALL-014 and CALL-015) because the question refers to customers who left.
'Customers who left' interpreted as churned customers; no company names were given so no entity resolution was needed.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: The connector gap was real. But it wasn't why we left. It was the thing we pointed at.
findings.context: Customer Kwame Boateng says the real reason Verity left was that nobody in operations built workflows; the connector gap was what they pointed at, not the true cause. — Stated reason differs from underlying reason; customer explicitly corrects Sarah's connector explanation

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: So we paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool.
findings.context: Verity bought OrbitFlow for business-user autonomy but every production workflow was built by engineering, so they paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. — Core reason for leaving; mismatch between pitch and use

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: Because we were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose main selling point was that we wouldn't have to maintain custom integrations.
findings.context: Engineering manager says the licence cost was being justified by business-user autonomy that wasn't materialising, and they were maintaining custom integrations despite the platform promising they would not have to. — Engineering-side reason for leaving

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: two of my engineers wanted to build it in-house and I spent eighteen months arguing against them, and eventually I ran out of arguments.
findings.context: Engineering team was split: Sarah's engineers wanted to build in-house, and she eventually ran out of arguments against that; Workato was chosen with positive engineering-facing reasons. — Contributing factor and tipping reason for choosing Workato

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: it's not primarily price.
findings.context: Workato was chosen over OrbitFlow partly for a stronger core banking connector and stronger engineering-facing story (recipes as code, CI); customer says pricing was only partly a factor and not primary. — Competitor moved to: Workato; price a secondary factor

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: Our settlement provider is a mid-sized European processor. You don't have a connector for them.
findings.context: Settlement reconciliation workflow could not be built economically because the settlement provider had no OrbitFlow connector and custom integration effort exceeded value. — Specific product gap raised as the February trigger; customer notes Workato also lacks the connector

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: Six of them never touched it again.
findings.context: Verity received limited enablement: a two-day onboarding for eight people, six never used it again, and no help until OrbitFlow offered paid sessions in January, which were declined. — Onboarding/adoption problem; OrbitFlow staff acknowledge hands-on service is paid add-on

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: if someone had sat with two of my people for a week in the first quarter and got them to ship something real, we'd still be a customer.
findings.context: Customer says hands-on build sessions would have kept them, but OrbitFlow's sitting-with-team service is a paid professional services engagement that was never offered to them. — Onboarding gap; Maya acknowledges the paid add-on may be the problem

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: We never had that and I never asked for it, because I thought the product removed the need for it.
findings.context: Verity never had a dedicated operations role to build and maintain automations; customer says the product was assumed to remove this need. — Root cause per customer; OrbitFlow staff say the product's operating model guidance states this but customer never saw it

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: That was an accurate and completely useless answer.
findings.context: Support quality was inconsistent, and Verity felt treated as a small account; a April connector request got only a template-not-found answer, while Workato's SE built a custom connector in three days unbilled during evaluation. — Contributing factor to leaving; not the primary reason per Sarah

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: You sold to my enthusiasm rather than to my capability.
findings.context: Customer says the sales process sold to their enthusiasm rather than their capability; nobody asked who would build workflows. — Sales-process criticism acknowledged by Maya

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: I think we were the wrong customer for the product, or the product was sold to us for the wrong reason.
findings.context: Customer says Verity was probably the wrong customer for the product, or was sold the product for the wrong reason. — Hedged overall view

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: Though I'd say the decision became inevitable in about February and it took us until June to admit it.
findings.context: Verity had decided internally by about February and formally in June; Workato evaluation started by March and gained momentum. — Timing of decision

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: Right. We bought something we didn't need. That's the whole answer.
findings.context: Customer says the core reason for leaving is that they bought a product they did not need; the purchase was oversized for a small team's automation needs. — Decision maker's primary explanation; customer states no product complaint.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: We were on Growth, at eighteen hundred a month, for thirty users, when we had four people who ever logged in.
findings.context: Customer was on Growth at £1,800/month for 30 users while only four people ever logged in. — Over-licensing relative to actual usage was the driver of the cost problem.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: About two thousand a year. Maybe two and a half with the tier we need.
findings.context: Customer is moving to Zapier at roughly £2,000–2,500 a year, about a tenth of the OrbitFlow cost. — Named competitor/replacement; cost is the main driver.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: They worked perfectly. That's the frustrating part. I've got no complaint about the product at all.
findings.context: Customer says the workflows worked perfectly and she has no product complaint. — Explicitly rules out product quality as the reason for leaving.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: We'll lose the approval steps and we'll lose the run history, which I'll genuinely miss.
findings.context: Customer acknowledges Zapier will lack approval steps and run history, and that Zapier cannot do contractor sign-off approval forms, which is a capability gap. — Hedge: capability loss accepted as worth less than the cost difference.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: We paid for eleven workflows' worth of value and a plan for forty.
findings.context: Customer says the original sale promised a scaling roadmap (compliance, service charges, contractor management) that never happened because the team lacked capacity; the purchase was priced against a future that did not occur. — Contributing factor: over-purchase based on sales-process roadmap; both sides were enthusiastic.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: If you'd had something at five or six hundred a month I'd still be a customer
findings.context: Customer says OrbitFlow should have flagged the unused seats after six months and that no smaller plan existed, which would have kept her as a customer. — Contributing factor: lack of proactive account monitoring and no entry tier below Growth.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: Your account was in a segment that doesn't get an assigned CSM.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff confirm there is no smaller plan than Growth and that the account was in a segment without an assigned CSM, so under-usage was not caught. — Vendor response explaining the lack of intervention.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: Nobody remembers how bad it was.
findings.context: Customer says the value faded over time: the pain the product solved stopped feeling urgent, and at renewal the invoice was questioned. — Contributing factor: value became invisible at renewal rather than a product failure.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: Fine. Genuinely fine.
findings.context: Customer says OrbitFlow's last-year service was fine and support tickets were answered; OrbitFlow contact was only a product announcement email. — Support not a reason for leaving; vendor outreach was thin.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: I probably should have pushed harder on whether you had the capacity for the roadmap we talked about.
findings.context: Alastair McCrae acknowledges he should have pressed on whether the customer had capacity for the roadmap sold. — Vendor admission about the sales process.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: With the approval forms, yes. Without them, no, because that's the bit Zapier can't do and it's the only thing I'll actually miss.
findings.context: Customer would only consider a smaller plan if it included approval forms; without them she would not buy. — Hypothetical retention condition.

draft.answer: Both churned customers say the product was mismatched to how they would actually use it, though the details differ. Verity Payments says the real cause was that no one in operations built workflows, so it paid for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool [C1][C2][C3]. Oakhill Property says it bought more than it needed and was over-licensed, and it is moving to a far cheaper Zapier setup [C5][C6][C7]. Contributing factors included enablement and support gaps, sales-process issues, and a competitor's engineering-facing strengths [C4][C8][C9][C10].

claims.text: Verity Payments' Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations) said the connector gap was real but was not why they left; it was "the thing we pointed at." He said the real cause was that nobody in operations built workflows and that Verity never had a dedicated operations role, because he thought the product removed that need.

Verity bought OrbitFlow for business-user autonomy, but engineering built every production workflow, so Kwame said they paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. Engineering manager Sarah Lindqvist said the licence cost was being justified by autonomy that wasn't materialising, and they were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose selling point was that they wouldn't have to.

Verity chose Workato partly for a stronger core banking connector and an engineering-facing story (recipes as code, CI). Kwame said price was not the primary reason. Some of Sarah's engineers also wanted to build in-house, and she ran out of arguments against it after eighteen months. The decision became inevitable around February and was formalised in June.

Verity also cited enablement and support problems. Onboarding was two days for eight people, six of whom never used the product again, and paid sessions offered in January were declined. Kwame said that if someone had sat with two of his people for a week in the first quarter, they'd still be a customer, and that the service was never offered to them. Sarah said support was inconsistent: an April connector request got an accurate but useless answer, while Workato's SE built a custom connector in three days unbilled. She did not call this the primary reason.

Oakhill Property's Hazel Wren (Operations Director) said the whole answer was that they bought something they didn't need. They were on Growth at £1,800/month for 30 users, and only four people ever logged in.
Hazel said the workflows worked perfectly and she has no product complaint. She also said the last year's service was fine.

Oakhill is moving to Zapier at about £2,000–2,500 a year, roughly a tenth of the OrbitFlow cost. Hazel accepts losing approval steps and run history, which she will miss, and Zapier can't do contractor sign-off approval forms.

Hazel said the original sale promised a scaling roadmap (compliance, service charges, contractor management) that never happened because the team lacked capacity. She said they paid for eleven workflows' worth of value and a plan for forty. Account Executive Alastair McCrae acknowledged he should have pushed harder on whether they had capacity for the roadmap.

Oakhill's value also faded over time: the pain the product solved stopped feeling urgent, and the invoice was questioned at renewal. Hazel said OrbitFlow should have flagged the unused seats and that a plan at £500–600/month would have kept her. OrbitFlow's Ruth Adeyemi confirmed there is no plan smaller than Growth and that the account was in a segment with no assigned CSM. Hazel would consider a smaller plan only if it included approval forms.

Kwame said Verity's sales process sold to their enthusiasm rather than their capability, and that nobody asked who would build workflows. He said Verity was probably the wrong customer, or was sold the product for the wrong reason.

Verity's trigger in February was that the settlement reconciliation workflow couldn't be built economically. The settlement provider had no OrbitFlow connector, and custom integration effort exceeded the value.

conflicts.description: Sarah raised the missing settlement-provider connector as the February trigger, while Kwame said the connector gap was only what they pointed at and not the real reason, which was that nobody in operations built workflows.

not_covered: Only two churn post-mortem calls (Verity Payments and Oakhill Property) were read, so this does not show how typical these reasons are across all churned customers.
